The flip side of this remarkable capacity for fast learning is that precise memories are quickly overwritten: recall performance for the original examples drops steeply over the first 10 training updates with new examples, followed by a more gradual decline. Even after 100K updates, however, some of the original examples are still recalled near perfectly. A qualitatively similar retention pattern has been observed in human long-term memory retention studies before (Bahrick, 1984). Finally, recognition is much more robust to interference than recall and memory for natural language sentences is generally superior to memory for stimuli without structure.

papers.title: Learning the Mechanism of Catastrophic Forgetting: A Perspective from Gradient Similarity
papers.research_question: What conditions lead to catastrophic forgetting? Which neurons are responsible for catastrophic forgetting? How to prevent catastrophic forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Establishes a gradient-based theoretical framework explaining catastrophic forgetting and proposes Collaborative Neuron Learning (CNL), which freezes conflicting neurons to prevent forgetting.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes a gradient-based theoretical framework for catastrophic forgetting, identifies conflicting and collaborative neurons, and proposes CNL which effectively prevents forgetting under ideal conditions and significantly reduces it in practical settings.
papers.key_findings:
Strongly negative gradient similarity is the fundamental cause of catastrophic forgetting.
Two types of neurons are identified: conflicting neurons (50-75% of all neurons) that induce forgetting, and collaborative neurons (25-50%) that mitigate forgetting.
CNL achieves zero forgetting under in-set experiments when the learning rate is infinitesimal and the Mastered Set is exactly known.
CNL reduces catastrophic forgetting by 59.1%–81.7% under out-of-set experiments.
CNL works with various optimizers (SGD, Momentum, Adam, AdamW) and on complex combined datasets.
papers.limitation: CNL achieves zero forgetting only under two restrictive conditions: sufficiently small learning rate and exactly known Mastered Set.
papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting during knowledge injection severely undermines the continual learning capability of large language models (LLMs). Although existing methods attempt to mitigate this issue, they often lack a foundational theoretical explanation. We establish a gradient-based theoretical framework to explain catastrophic forgetting. We first prove that strongly negative gradient similarity is a fundamental cause of forgetting. We then use gradient similarity to identify two types of neurons: conflicting neurons that induce forgetting and account for 50%-75% of neurons, and collaborative neurons that mitigate forgetting and account for 25%-50%. Based on this analysis, we propose a knowledge injection method, Collaborative Neural Learning (CNL). By freezing conflicting neurons and updating only collaborative neurons, CNL theoretically eliminates catastrophic forgetting under an infinitesimal learning rate eta and an exactly known mastered set. Experiments on five LLMs, four datasets, and four optimizers show that CNL achieves zero forgetting in in-set settings and reduces forgetting by 59.1%-81.7% in out-of-set settings.

papers.title: Contextual Gradient Interference: A Novel Mechanism for Knowledge Retention and Adaptability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in large language models by enabling knowledge retention while adapting to new tasks through a gradient-based mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Contextual Gradient Interference mechanism, a dual-gradient framework that dynamically partitions parameter updates to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and enhance knowledge retention and adaptability in large language models.
papers.conclusion: The Contextual Gradient Interference mechanism successfully addresses catastrophic forgetting by balancing knowledge preservation and task adaptation, demonstrating improved performance and scalability in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
The CGI mechanism improves accuracy, reduces perplexity, and enhances retention scores across various tasks.
It outperforms baseline models in retention scores for sequential learning tasks.
The model shows adaptability to variable contexts, though performance declines with increased complexity in multi-hop reasoning.
Scalability tests show accuracy plateaus beyond 100GB dataset size, with training time increasing non-linearly.
The model is robust to noisy inputs but accuracy decreases with higher noise levels.
papers.limitation:
Increased computational overhead associated with gradient decomposition and real-time masking
Reliance on auxiliary loss functions requiring careful hyperparameter calibration
Sensitivity to input quality under noisy conditions
future_direction: Investigating alternative methods for gradient decomposition, such as sparse or low-rank approximations
Incorporating reinforcement learning paradigms to dynamically adjust masking parameters based on task feedback
Exploring integration with emerging architectures, such as sparse attention or memory-augmented transformers
papers.abstract: Addressing the challenge of catastrophic forgetting in large-scale neural architectures requires innovative solutions that enable models to retain prior knowledge while adapting to new tasks. The proposed Contextual Gradient Interference mechanism introduces a dual-gradient framework designed to partition parameter updates dynamically, ensuring stability for previously learned information while facilitating effective task-specific adaptations. By leveraging real-time gradient analysis and masking strategies, the mechanism mitigates interference and promotes efficient learning across sequential tasks. The integration of this approach within the Falcon model, a state-of-the-art open-source language model, demonstrated significant improvements in knowledge retention, task adaptability, and robustness under varying conditions, including noisy inputs and increasing dataset sizes. Quantitative evaluations across multiple benchmarks revealed enhanced accuracy, lower perplexity, and improved memory retention compared to existing methodologies. The scalability of the approach was further validated through its computational efficiency and performance consistency over extended training cycles. Additional experiments highlighted the ability of the model to handle multi-hop reasoning and sequential tasks with complex contextual dependencies, showcasing the versatility of the proposed mechanism. An ablation study reinforced the significance of key components, such as gradient masking and decomposition, in achieving the observed performance gains. Results also revealed areas for potential optimization, including computational trade-offs and sensitivity to hyperparameter configurations. The study advances the understanding of gradient-based learning strategies and their critical role in optimizing neural networks for dynamic and large-scale tasks. Through its novel contributions, the mechanism establishes a foundation for enhancing the stability, adaptability, and efficiency of language model training, making it an invaluable tool for future developments in machine learning.

papers.title: Mechanism and Emergence of Stacked Attention Heads in Multi-Layer Transformers
papers.research_question: What tasks require transformers of a specific depth? Can large language models solve such tasks without fine-tuning? What mechanism do transformers use to solve the task? How does this mechanism emerge during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the retrieval problem, a task requiring a minimum number of transformer layers, and uncovers that transformers solve it using stacked attention heads (retrieval heads) which emerge gradually via an implicit curriculum.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces the retrieval problem, shows it requires a certain number of layers, and finds transformers solve it using a mechanism resembling an induction head that emerges gradually with the help of an implicit curriculum.
papers.key_findings:
The retrieval problem requires a minimum number of transformer layers that grows logarithmically with the number of retrieval steps.
Large language models can solve the retrieval problem without any specific fine-tuning.
Transformers solve the retrieval problem using stacked attention heads that resemble induction heads.
Retrieval heads emerge gradually during training, one head at a time, guided by an implicit curriculum.
The implicit curriculum is essential for successful learning of the retrieval problem.
papers.limitation:
The analysis of transformers trained on a minimal formulation of the retrieval problem might not generalize perfectly to large language models.
The paper does not provide a full explanation of the training dynamics of transformers on the retrieval problem.
future_direction: Further research is needed to fully understand the multi-layered circuits learned by large language models and the training dynamics that enable their learning.
papers.abstract: In this paper, I introduce the retrieval problem, a simple yet common reasoning task that can be solved only by transformers with a minimum number of layers, which grows logarithmically with the input size. I empirically show that large language models can solve the task under different prompting formulations without any fine-tuning. To understand how transformers solve the retrieval problem, I train several transformers on a minimal formulation. Successful learning occurs only under the presence of an implicit curriculum. I uncover the learned mechanisms by studying the attention maps in the trained transformers. I also study the training process, uncovering that attention heads always emerge in a specific sequence guided by the implicit curriculum.

papers.title: Learning to Remember from a Multi-Task Teacher
papers.research_question: How can we reduce catastrophic forgetting at the representation level in sequential learning, and can a meta-learning algorithm that mimics a multi-task teacher's representation achieve this?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a measure of catastrophic forgetting at the representation level using a linear readout layer and introduces a meta-learning algorithm that learns weight updates to mimic a multi-task teacher's representation, thereby reducing representational forgetting in sequential learning.
papers.conclusion: The proposed meta-learner can overcome catastrophic forgetting while improving performance on new tasks and generalizes to unseen classes, initializations, and domains, though scaling to longer sequences remains a challenge.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed meta-learner significantly reduces representational forgetting on old tasks while maintaining good performance on new tasks.
The meta-learner generalizes to unseen classes, unseen network initialization checkpoints, and unseen data domains (e.g., from CIFAR to Tiny-ImageNet).
The meta-learner can handle sequential learning with more than two tasks, though performance on intermediate tasks is not as strong as on the first task.
The meta-learner's output (gradient multiplier) is non-trivial and can sometimes be negative, indicating it learns to dynamically modify gradient directions to prevent forgetting.
Representational forgetting, measured by a linear readout layer, shows a significant drop in performance on old tasks even when the output layer is re-learned, indicating that forgetting occurs at the representation level.
papers.limitation: The meta-learner currently generalizes well up to 600 steps but finds it challenging to generalize to even longer sequences.
future_direction: Training the meta-learner with longer sequences and more sequential tasks with more computational resources.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning typically focus on fixing the accuracy of the predictions for a previously learned task. In this paper we argue that the outputs of neural networks are subject to rapid changes when learning a new data distribution, and networks that appear to "forget" everything still contain useful representation towards previous tasks. Instead of enforcing the output accuracy to stay the same, we propose to reduce the effect of catastrophic forgetting on the representation level, as the output layer can be quickly recovered later with a small number of examples. Towards this goal, we propose an experimental setup that measures the amount of representational forgetting, and develop a novel meta-learning algorithm to overcome this issue. The proposed meta-learner produces weight updates of a sequential learning network, mimicking a multi-task teacher network's representation. We show that our meta-learner can improve its learned representations on new tasks, while maintaining a good representation for old tasks.

papers.title: Gradient Localization Improves Lifelong Pretraining of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can gradient localization be used to improve continual pretraining of language models for temporal knowledge updates and reduce catastrophic forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Traced Gradient Layers (TGL), a method that uses gradient norms to identify and target specific layers during continual pretraining, improving knowledge uptake and reducing forgetting.
papers.conclusion: The proposed TGL method improves continual pretraining by localizing gradient updates to relevant layers, as demonstrated on knowledge probing tasks without requiring fine-grained annotations.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient norms for knowledge-intensive salient spans are significantly higher in specific layers compared to standard pretraining.
Targeting updates to layers with high relative gradient norms improves performance on temporal knowledge probing tasks.
TGL methods can be applied on top of existing continual learning techniques to enhance their effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
It is unclear whether improvements in knowledge probe perplexity transfer to downstream settings.
Reductions in pretraining cost may lead to increased model pretraining due to Jevons Paradox.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) trained on web-scale text corpora have been shown to capture world knowledge in their parameters. However, the mechanism by which language models store different types of knowledge is poorly understood. In this work, we examine two types of knowledge relating to temporally sensitive entities and demonstrate that each type is localized to different sets of parameters within the LLMs. We hypothesize that the lack of consideration of the locality of knowledge in existing continual learning methods contributes to both: the failed uptake of new information, and catastrophic forgetting of previously learned information. We observe that sequences containing references to updated and newly mentioned entities exhibit larger gradient norms in a subset of layers. We demonstrate that targeting parameter updates to these relevant layers can improve the performance of continually pretraining on language containing temporal drift.

papers.title: Understanding Verbatim Memorization in LLMs Through Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: What specific circuits in the model are responsible for initiating and maintaining verbatim memorization, and how do they differ from non-memorized generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using contrastive datasets and circuit discovery to identify circuits responsible for memorization in LLMs, finding that initiation circuits can also maintain memorization, but maintenance circuits cannot initiate it, and that memorization prevention transfers across domains while induction is context-dependent.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that memorization initiation and maintenance are handled by different circuits, with initiation circuits being more general and maintenance circuits being more specific. Memorization prevention transfers across domains, while induction is context-dependent.
papers.key_findings:
Created two distinct contrastive datasets for memorization decision and branch comparison tasks.
Discovered compact circuits (≤5% of model edges) for memorization decision and branch comparison tasks using attribution patching techniques.
Circuits that initiate memorization can also maintain it once started, while circuits that only maintain memorization cannot trigger its initiation.
Memorization prevention mechanisms transfer robustly across different text domains (GitHub, Enron Emails, Common Crawl), while memorization induction appears more context-dependent.
Removing memorization (noising approach) is easier than inducing memorization (denoising approach) in the studied setup.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on Edge Attribution Patching with Integrated Gradients (EAP-IG) for circuit discovery, which provides only an approximation and may not fully correlate with direct activation patching measurements.
Findings are limited to a single, relatively small language model (GPT-Neo-125m); larger models might employ more complex or differently distributed memorization mechanisms.
Uncertainty about whether the identified circuits represent general memorization mechanisms or are specific to the Wikipedia subset of The Pile or artifacts of the contrastive dataset construction.
future_direction: Investigate how memorization mechanisms scale with model size.
Explore whether similar circuits exist in different model architectures.
Expand testing to more diverse datasets and memorization criteria to establish the generality of these mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Underlying mechanisms of memorization in LLMs-the verbatim reproduction of training data-remain poorly understood.What exact part of the network decides to retrieve a token that we would consider as start of memorization sequence?How exactly is the models' behaviour different when producing memorized sentence vs non-memorized?In this work we approach these questions from mechanistic interpretability standpoint by utilizing transformer circuits-the minimal computational subgraphs that perform specific functions within the model.Through carefully constructed contrastive datasets, we identify points where model generation diverges from memorized content and isolate the specific circuits responsible for two distinct aspects of memorization.We find that circuits that initiate memorization can also maintain it once started, while circuits that only maintain memorization cannot trigger its initiation.Intriguingly, memorization prevention mechanisms transfer robustly across different text domains, while memorization induction appears more contextdependent. 1

papers.title: Lost in the Middle: An Emergent Property from Information Retrieval Demands in LLMs
papers.research_question: Why do LLMs exhibit the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon (U-shaped performance curve)? The paper investigates whether this behavior emerges from adaptations to short-term and long-term information retrieval demands during training.
papers.core_contribution: The lost-in-the-middle behavior in LLMs emerges from joint optimization on short-term and long-term information retrieval demands, and is influenced by architectural biases (autoregressive design) and attention sinks.
papers.conclusion: The lost-in-the-middle phenomenon is an emergent property from information retrieval demands, influenced by model architecture and attention dynamics, rather than a simple flaw.
papers.key_findings:
Training on free recall (long-term demand) yields primacy, on running span (short-term demand) yields recency, and joint training yields the U-shaped lost-in-the-middle curve.
Primacy effect arises from uniform long-term demand and is shaped by autoregressive architecture (causal masking), as shown by comparison with T5.
Recency effect directly aligns with the shape of short-term demand in training data.
Attention sinks support primacy under long-term memory demand; ablating them impairs free recall but not running span.
The effects generalize to masked sequence completion tasks, which more closely resemble next-token prediction.
future_direction: Uncovering connections between artificial and biological systems in memory phenomena.
papers.abstract: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) often degrades when crucial information is in the middle of a long context, a "lost-in-the-middle" phenomenon that mirrors the primacy and recency effects in human memory. We propose that this behavior is not simply a flaw indicative of information loss but an adaptation to different information retrieval demands during pre-training: some tasks require uniform recall across the entire input (a long-term memory demand), while others prioritize the most recent information (a short-term memory demand). Consistent with this view, we show that this U-shaped performance curve emerges when LLMs (GPT-2 and Llama variants) are trained from scratch on two simple human memory paradigms simulating long-term and short-term memory demands. Our analysis reveals that while the recency effect directly aligns with short-term memory demand in the training data, the primacy effect is induced by the uniform long-term memory demand and is additionally influenced by the model's autoregressive properties and the formation of attention sinks. Our main findings from simple human memory paradigms also generalize to a sequence completion task, which more closely resembles the next-token prediction process in LLM pre-training. Together, our findings reveal how information retrieval demands, model architecture, and structural attention dynamics during model training can jointly produce positional bias observed in LLMs.

papers.title: Probing Across Time: What Does RoBERTa Know and When?
papers.research_question: For various types of knowledge a language model learns, when during (pre)training are they acquired?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a probing across time framework and finds that during pretraining, linguistic knowledge is acquired fast and stably, factual and commonsense knowledge slower and more domain-sensitive, and reasoning abilities are largely not stably acquired.
papers.conclusion: RoBERTa learns linguistic knowledge faster than factual and commonsense knowledge, but struggles to learn reasoning abilities. The probing across time framework can serve as a general framework to inform progress on models and probes.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic knowledge is acquired fast, stably, and robustly across domains.
Factual and commonsense knowledge are acquired slower and are more domain-sensitive.
Reasoning abilities are largely not stably acquired.
The learning order and patterns hold regardless of data variation (domain and size), but domain diversity is more important than quantity.
Benchmark tasks that require complex knowledge (e.g., ReCoRD, WSC) benefit from longer pretraining, aligning with probing results.
papers.limitation:
Changes to hyperparameters might lead to different conclusions.
Differences in pretraining setup (e.g., batch size, data) may cause performance degradation compared to original RoBERTa.
future_direction: Exploration of different objectives and architectures (e.g., GPT-2).
More efficient pretraining by understanding when necessary knowledge is acquired.
Understanding dependencies among different kinds of knowledge.
papers.abstract: Models of language trained on very large corpora have been demonstrated useful for NLP. As fixed artifacts, they have become the object of intense study, with many researchers "probing" the extent to which linguistic abstractions, factual and commonsense knowledge, and reasoning abilities they acquire and readily demonstrate. Building on this line of work, we consider a new question: for types of knowledge a language model learns, when during (pre)training are they acquired? We plot probing performance across iterations, using RoBERTa as a case study. Among our findings: linguistic knowledge is acquired fast, stably, and robustly across domains. Facts and commonsense are slower and more domain-sensitive. Reasoning abilities are, in general, not stably acquired. As new datasets, pretraining protocols, and probes emerge, we believe that probing-across-time analyses can help researchers understand the complex, intermingled learning that these models undergo and guide us toward more efficient approaches that accomplish necessary learning faster.

papers.title: Toward Understanding Unlearning Difficulty: A Mechanistic Perspective and Circuit-Guided Difficulty Metric
papers.research_question: Can we define and quantify a sample’s unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective before unlearning? Can this predicted difficulty be linked to the internal mechanisms (e.g. circuits) within the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Circuit-guided Unlearning Difficulty (CUD), a metric to quantify sample-level unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective before unlearning, based on circuit-level signals.
papers.conclusion: CUD is a reliable metric for quantifying unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective, enabling proactive identification of easy and hard samples and promoting difficulty-aware unlearning methods.
papers.key_findings:
CUD reliably separates intrinsically easy and hard samples for unlearning and remains stable across unlearning methods.
CUD is robust to the choice of similarity metric and loss function used in its construction.
Easy-to-unlearn samples are associated with shorter, shallower circuits concentrated in earlier-to-intermediate layers.
Hard-to-unlearn samples rely on longer and deeper pathways closer to late-stage computation and output layers.
CUD provides a continuous, pre-unlearning difficulty score that is distinct from post-hoc measures like MRD.
papers.limitation: CUD may be computationally expensive due to the need for circuit discovery.
future_direction: Using CUD to construct controlled forget sets at specified difficulty levels for benchmarking.
Designing curriculum-style unlearning schedules based on difficulty.
Developing efficient approximations of CUD.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is becoming essential for building trustworthy and compliant language models. Yet unlearning success varies considerably across individual samples: some are reliably erased, while others persist despite the same procedure. We argue that this disparity is not only a data-side phenomenon, but also reflects model-internal mechanisms that encode and protect memorized information. We study this problem from a mechanistic perspective based on model circuits--structured interaction pathways that govern how predictions are formed. We propose Circuit-guided Unlearning Difficulty (CUD), a {\em pre-unlearning} metric that assigns each sample a continuous difficulty score using circuit-level signals. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CUD reliably separates intrinsically easy and hard samples, and remains stable across unlearning methods. We identify key circuit-level patterns that reveal a mechanistic signature of difficulty: easy-to-unlearn samples are associated with shorter, shallower interactions concentrated in earlier-to-intermediate parts of the original model, whereas hard samples rely on longer and deeper pathways closer to late-stage computation. Compared to existing qualitative studies, CUD takes a first step toward a principled, fine-grained, and interpretable analysis of unlearning difficulty; and motivates the development of unlearning methods grounded in model mechanisms.

papers.title: Understanding Transformer Memorization Recall Through Idioms
papers.research_question: When does a model decide to output a memorized phrase, and how is this phrase then retrieved from memory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a methodological framework and dataset for probing memorization recall in transformers, and finds that memorized predictions involve a two-step process of candidate promotion in early layers and confidence boosting in upper layers.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our work makes a first step towards understanding memory recall, and provides a methodological basis for future studies of transformer memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Memorized predictions are a two-step process: early layers promote the predicted token to the top of the output distribution, and upper layers increase model confidence.
Memorized information is stored and retrieved in the early layers of the network.
The first layer is especially critical for memorized predictions.
The findings generalize from idioms to factual statements.
The IDIO MEM dataset is constructed for probing memorization and released for the community.
papers.abstract: To produce accurate predictions, language models (LMs) must balance between generalization and memorization. Yet, little is known about the mechanism by which transformer LMs employ their memorization capacity. When does a model decide to output a memorized phrase, and how is this phrase then retrieved from memory? In this work, we offer the first methodological framework for probing and characterizing recall of memorized sequences in transformer LMs. First, we lay out criteria for detecting model inputs that trigger memory recall, and propose idioms as inputs that typically fulfill these criteria. Next, we construct a dataset of English idioms and use it to compare model behavior on memorized vs. non-memorized inputs. Specifically, we analyze the internal prediction construction process by interpreting the model's hidden representations as a gradual refinement of the output probability distribution. We find that across different model sizes and architectures, memorized predictions are a two-step process: early layers promote the predicted token to the top of the output distribution, and upper layers increase model confidence. This suggests that memorized information is stored and retrieved in the early layers of the network. Last, we demonstrate the utility of our methodology beyond idioms in memorized factual statements. Overall, our work makes a first step towards understanding memory recall, and provides a methodological basis for future studies of transformer memorization.

papers.title: LMEnt: A Suite for Analyzing Knowledge in Language Models from Pretraining Data to Representations
papers.research_question: How do language models acquire and represent knowledge from pretraining data, and what is the interplay between data composition, training dynamics, and internal knowledge mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LMEnt, a suite for analyzing knowledge acquisition in language models, including annotated pretraining data, entity-based retrieval, and pretrained models, enabling studies on the connection between data and knowledge representations.
papers.conclusion: LMEnt provides a flexible testbed for investigating knowledge representations in language models and facilitates future research on knowledge acquisition and editing.
papers.key_findings:
LMEnt's entity-based retrieval outperforms string-based methods by up to 80.4% in returning relevant document chunks.
LMEnt models achieve comparable knowledge recall performance to models trained on orders of magnitude more data.
Knowledge acquisition is correlated with fact frequency, but both learning and forgetting rates increase with frequency.
Increasing model size improves learning of frequent facts but has little effect on tail facts.
papers.limitation:
Pretraining data is relatively small and models are compute-efficient, which may limit generalizability.
Does not compare with dense retrievers like DPR or ColBERT.
Focuses only on pretraining, not mid- or post-training phases.
future_direction: Investigating knowledge plasticity and editing during pretraining.
Improving factuality of LMs using entity annotations.
Extending LMEnt to other data sources and architectures.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) increasingly drive real-world applications that require world knowledge. However, the internal processes through which models turn data into representations of knowledge and beliefs about the world, are poorly understood. Insights into these processes could pave the way for developing LMs with knowledge representations that are more consistent, robust, and complete. To facilitate studying these questions, we present LMEnt, a suite for analyzing knowledge acquisition in LMs during pretraining. LMEnt introduces: (1) a knowledge-rich pretraining corpus, fully annotated with entity mentions, based on Wikipedia, (2) an entity-based retrieval method over pretraining data that outperforms previous approaches by as much as 80.4%, and (3) 12 pretrained models with up to 1B parameters and 4K intermediate checkpoints, with comparable performance to popular open-sourced models on knowledge benchmarks. Together, these resources provide a controlled environment for analyzing connections between entity mentions in pretraining and downstream performance, and the effects of causal interventions in pretraining data. We show the utility of LMEnt by studying knowledge acquisition across checkpoints, finding that fact frequency is key, but does not fully explain learning trends. We release LMEnt to support studies of knowledge in LMs, including knowledge representations, plasticity, editing, attribution, and learning dynamics.

papers.title: Dissecting Fine-Tuning Unlearning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do fine-tuning-based unlearning methods appear successful in behavioral tests, and what is their actual mechanism and limitations?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods do not genuinely erase problematic knowledge; instead, they alter the model's knowledge retrieval process by modifying the coefficients in the MLP's final layers, which also negatively impacts unrelated knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods do not erase knowledge but alter knowledge extraction mechanisms, and they negatively impact the model's unrelated capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Restoring the value vectors in MLPs does not recover unlearned knowledge, indicating that the knowledge remains stored.
Restoring the attention states in intermediate and deeper layers recovers some knowledge, showing that attention components are involved in knowledge extraction.
Restoring the coefficients in the final layers of MLPs recovers most of the unlearned knowledge, indicating that these coefficients are the primary contributors to the unlearning effect.
Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods have a global negative effect, degrading the model's performance on unrelated knowledge.
The unlearning mechanism works by altering the model's knowledge retrieval process rather than erasing the knowledge itself.
papers.limitation: The experiments disregard potential unlearning impact from parameter changes in other model components (e.g., unembedding matrix and normalization layers), and it is unclear if these changes have meaningful effects.
future_direction: Future unlearning evaluations should focus on precise measurement of knowledge storage and retrieval dynamics.
Further investigation into defensive strategies based on the findings about MLP coefficients.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods prevail for preventing targeted harmful, sensitive, or copyrighted information within large language models while preserving overall capabilities. However, the true effectiveness of these methods is unclear. In this work, we delve into the limitations of fine-tuning-based unlearning through activation patching and parameter restoration experiments. Our findings reveal that these methods alter the model's knowledge retrieval process, providing further evidence that they do not genuinely erase the problematic knowledge embedded in the model parameters. Instead, the coefficients generated by the MLP components in the model's final layer are the primary contributors to these seemingly positive unlearning effects, playing a crucial role in controlling the model's behaviors. Furthermore, behavioral tests demonstrate that this unlearning mechanism inevitably impacts the global behavior of the models, affecting unrelated knowledge or capabilities. The code is released at https://github.com/yihuaihong/Dissecting-FT-Unlearning.

papers.title: Filtering with Self-Attention and Storing with MLP: One-Layer Transformers Can Provably Acquire and Extract Knowledge
papers.research_question: How do transformers acquire knowledge during pre-training via next-token prediction and extract it after fine-tuning? Under what conditions can pre-trained transformers perform out-of-distribution generalization after full and low-rank fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a theoretical framework for one-layer transformers that shows they can achieve near-optimal pre-training loss and post-fine-tuning out-of-distribution generalization under certain conditions, and explains the roles of self-attention and MLP in knowledge acquisition and extraction.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework provides convergence and generalization guarantees for one-layer transformers, elucidating the mechanisms of knowledge acquisition and extraction and the conditions for successful out-of-distribution generalization after fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can achieve near-optimal pre-training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition.
Given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction.
Violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations.
Self-attention learns to filter out noise tokens and focus on subject and relation tokens, enabling the MLP to learn balanced features for subjects and relations.
Low-rank fine-tuning is effective because the fine-tuning gradients closely approximate their best rank-1 form, with the right singular vector aligning with the Q&A format embedding.
papers.limitation: Uses orthogonal embeddings and simplified architecture, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Analysis of random embeddings instead of orthogonal embeddings.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) demonstrate exceptional performance on knowledge-intensive tasks, yet the theoretical mechanisms underlying knowledge acquisition (storage and memorization) during pre-training and extraction (retrieval and recall) during inference after fine-tuning remain poorly understood. Although prior theoretical studies have explored these processes through analyses of training dynamics, they overlook critical components essential for a comprehensive theory: (1) the multi-layer perceptron (MLP), empirically identified as the primary module for knowledge storage; (2) out-of-distribution (OOD) adaptivity, which enables LLMs to generalize to unseen scenarios post-pre-training; and (3) next-token prediction, the standard autoregressive objective that encodes knowledge as conditional probabilities. In this work, we introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first theoretical framework that addresses these limitations by examining the training dynamics of one-layer transformers. Under regularity assumptions, we establish that: (i) transformers attain near-optimal training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition; (ii) given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction; and (iii) violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations. Our analysis encompasses both full fine-tuning and low-rank fine-tuning, yielding insights into the efficacy of practical low-rank adaptation methods. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on synthetic datasets and the real-world PopQA benchmark, employing GPT-2 and Llama-3.2-1B models.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Model Organisms for Human Associative Learning
papers.research_question: Do LLMs exhibit representational dynamics akin to human associative learning, and can they help disambiguate between competing hypotheses for representational change? How does vocabulary interference modulate representational change?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs exhibit a non-monotonic pattern of representational change during associative learning (consistent with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis), and this change is modulated by vocabulary interference, with higher interference leading to stronger differentiation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can serve as accessible and general computational models for studying human associative learning, providing new insights into how local pair similarity and global competition shape representational change.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show three distinct phases of learning during in-context associative learning: encoding (accuracy increases), consolidation (accuracy stabilizes), and forgetting (accuracy declines).
During the consolidation phase, moderately similar token pairs significantly differentiate, producing a U-shaped pattern of representational change that aligns with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis.
Vocabulary interference—the similarity between a paired item and the model's prior knowledge—modulates representational change: higher interference leads to stronger differentiation.
The non-monotonic differentiation pattern is only present during consolidation and disappears during encoding and forgetting phases.
These representational dynamics are consistent across six different open-source LLMs, despite architectural differences.
papers.limitation:
The token pairs used are synthetic and optimized for similarity, which may not reflect naturalistic learning scenarios.
The forgetting phase is not well understood, and its causes require further investigation.
LLMs are not biologically plausible models of the brain, limiting direct comparisons to neural mechanisms.
future_direction: Investigating the causes of forgetting and predicting when it occurs.
Extending the analysis to more naturalistic stimuli and real-world associative learning tasks.
Exploring how different model architectures (e.g., with explicit memory modules) affect representational dynamics.
papers.abstract: Associative learning--forming links between co-occurring items--is fundamental to human cognition, reshaping internal representations in complex ways. Testing hypotheses on how representational changes occur in biological systems is challenging, but large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable alternative. Building on LLMs' in-context learning, we adapt a cognitive neuroscience associative learning paradigm and investigate how representations evolve across six models. Our initial findings reveal a non-monotonic pattern consistent with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis, with moderately similar items differentiating after learning. Leveraging the controllability of LLMs, we further show that this differentiation is modulated by the overlap of associated items with the broader vocabulary--a factor we term vocabulary interference, capturing how new associations compete with prior knowledge. We find that higher vocabulary interference amplifies differentiation, suggesting that representational change is influenced by both item similarity and global competition. Our findings position LLMs not only as powerful tools for studying representational dynamics in human-like learning systems, but also as accessible and general computational models for generating new hypotheses about the principles underlying memory reorganization in the brain.

papers.title: Time Course MechInterp: Analyzing the Evolution of Components and Knowledge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Which components (attention heads, FFNs) contribute to solving factual knowledge tasks, and how do these circuits for factual knowledge evolve over the course of model training?
papers.core_contribution: This work provides a mechanistic view of how factual knowledge representation evolves during LLM pre-training, showing that models initially rely on general-purpose components which later specialize, with attention heads exhibiting high turnover and FFNs remaining more stable.
papers.conclusion: The study offers insights into the hierarchical learning process of LLMs, where general components form first and later diversify, with attention heads being highly adaptive and FFNs providing stable processing.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads show high turnover and dynamic role transitions, while FFNs are more stable throughout training.
Location-based relations (LOC) converge to high accuracy earlier in training than name-based relations (NAME).
LLMs initially depend on broad, general-purpose components, which later specialize as training progresses.
Answer-specific attention heads demonstrate the highest turnover, indicating frequent role changes.
FFNs act as a steady processing backbone, with most remaining in general roles.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints prevented analysis at the neuron level and the use of alternative interpretability techniques like activation patching across all snapshots.
The dataset is limited to English and covers only location-based and name-based factual relations.
The analysis uses a fixed activation threshold for role classification, which may introduce bias.
Only a subset of training snapshots was analyzed, leaving gaps in tracking role transitions.
Direct comparison with other model families (e.g., Pythia) was not feasible due to architectural differences preventing the use of IFRs.
future_direction: Incorporate more diverse datasets, additional model variants, and alternative interpretability techniques.
Expand analysis to other domains, multilingual settings, and ambiguous queries.
Investigate the long-term impact of component dynamics on fine-tuning, pruning, and continual learning.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) acquire and store factual knowledge is crucial for enhancing their interpretability and reliability.In this work, we analyze the evolution of factual knowledge representation in the OLMo-7B model by tracking the roles of its attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) over the course of pre-training.We classify these components into four roles: general, entity, relation-answer, and fact-answer specific and examine their stability and transitions.Our results show that LLMs initially depend on broad, general-purpose components, which later specialize as training progresses.Once the model reliably predicts answers, some components are repurposed, suggesting an adaptive learning process.Notably, attention heads display the highest turnover.We also present evidence that FFNs remain more stable throughout training.Furthermore, our probing experiments reveal that location-based relations converge to high accuracy earlier in training than namebased relations, highlighting how task complexity shapes acquisition dynamics.These insights offer a mechanistic view of knowledge formation in LLMs.We release the code and data. 1

papers.title: Neuron-Level Differentiation of Memorization and Generalization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do distinct sets of neurons underlie memorization and generalization behaviors in LLMs? Can targeted neuron-level interventions at inference time steer model behavior toward memorization or generalization? Are the observed neuron-behavior associations consistent across retraining runs and transferable across different tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that memorization and generalization activate distinct neuron subsets within LLMs, and that intervening on these subsets can controllably alter model behavior, with these neuron-behavior mappings being stable across intra-task and inter-task variations.
papers.conclusion: Memorization and generalization are encoded in separable neural pathways within LLMs, enabling inference-time steering and revealing consistent functional modularity.
papers.key_findings:
Distinct neuron subsets are responsible for memorization and generalization behaviors in LLMs.
Inference-time interventions on these neurons can steer the model's behavior toward memorization or generalization.
The neuron-behavior associations are consistent across retraining runs on the same task (intra-task consistency).
Neurons identified from one task can transfer to another task to some extent (inter-task transferability).
Behavior-associated signals originate primarily in the pretrained base model rather than the LoRA adapter.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to GPT-2 and LLaMA 3.2 models, lacking validation on diverse architectures and scales.
Evaluation uses only two task types (induction-style in-context inference and arithmetic addition), not capturing the breadth of language tasks.
The operationalization of generalization is comparatively less complete than memorization, capturing only specific forms.
The inference-time intervention uses a straightforward linear neuron-shifting method, which may not be optimal.
future_direction: Broader validation on diverse architectures and scales.
Examination of more varied tasks such as QA, commonsense reasoning, or dialogue.
Development of improved neuron selection methods for higher behavioral specificity.
papers.abstract: We investigate how Large Language Models (LLMs) distinguish between memorization and generalization at the neuron level. Through carefully designed tasks, we identify distinct neuron subsets responsible for each behavior. Experiments on both a GPT-2 model trained from scratch and a pretrained LLaMA-3.2 model fine-tuned with LoRA show consistent neuron-level specialization. We further demonstrate that inference-time interventions on these neurons can steer the model's behavior toward memorization or generalization. To assess robustness, we evaluate intra-task and inter-task consistency, confirming that these neuron-behavior associations reflect generalizable patterns rather than dataset-specific artifacts. Our findings reveal modular structure in LLMs and enable controlling memorization and generalization behaviors at inference time.

papers.title: Aspects of human memory and Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do Large Language Models exhibit human-like memory properties such as primacy and recency effects, and are these properties due to architectural biases or learned from training data?
papers.core_contribution: Large Language Models exhibit human-like memory properties such as primacy and recency effects, and these properties are likely learned from the statistical patterns in training data rather than being inherent to the transformer architecture.
papers.conclusion: The human-like memory properties observed in Large Language Models are likely learned from statistical patterns in human-generated text, suggesting that human memory characteristics influence the structure of narratives.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit primacy and recency effects in memory recall.
Adding elaborations to facts improves recall accuracy.
Forgetting in LLMs occurs primarily through interference rather than memory decay.
Repetitions improve recall, with spaced repetitions being more effective than immediate ones.
LLMs show a 'memory formation time' where recall improves with initial distance from the presented facts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are huge artificial neural networks which primarily serve to generate text, but also provide a very sophisticated probabilistic model of language use. Since generating a semantically consistent text requires a form of effective memory, we investigate the memory properties of LLMs and find surprising similarities with key characteristics of human memory. We argue that the human-like memory properties of the Large Language Model do not follow automatically from the LLM architecture but are rather learned from the statistics of the training textual data. These results strongly suggest that the biological features of human memory leave an imprint on the way that we structure our textual narratives.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: The Rise of Parameter Specialization for Knowledge Storage in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the way knowledge is stored in MLP parameters and the performance of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Stronger large language models exhibit higher parameter specialization for knowledge storage in MLPs, and this specialization improves the efficiency of knowledge utilization and reduces hallucination.
papers.conclusion: Enhanced parameter specialization for knowledge storage correlates with superior performance in LLMs, and optimizing this specialization improves task performance and reduces hallucination, highlighting the importance of aligning knowledge storage with retrieval mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Stronger models show higher parameter specialization, with PSS correlating strongly with performance on knowledge tasks.
Parameter specialization increases with model scale within the same family.
Parameter specialization evolves during pretraining, increasing in later training steps.
Fine-tuning that enhances parameter specialization (FT-PV) improves performance on knowledge tasks and reduces hallucination compared to other fine-tuning strategies.
Specialized knowledge distribution helps compress knowledge and reduce interference from irrelevant information.
papers.limitation:
Only examined knowledge parameter specialization within the MLP, not attention modules.
Tested models only up to 14B parameters due to GPU limitations.
future_direction: Progressively narrow the focus to individual neurons to measure more precise Parameter Specialization.
Extend the concept to other model architectures like Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Sparse Auto-Encoders (SAEs).
papers.abstract: Over time, a growing wave of large language models from various series has been introduced to the community. Researchers are striving to maximize the performance of language models with constrained parameter sizes. However, from a microscopic perspective, there has been limited research on how to better store knowledge in model parameters, particularly within MLPs, to enable more effective utilization of this knowledge by the model. In this work, we analyze twenty publicly available open-source large language models to investigate the relationship between their strong performance and the way knowledge is stored in their corresponding MLP parameters. Our findings reveal that as language models become more advanced and demonstrate stronger knowledge capabilities, their parameters exhibit increased specialization. Specifically, parameters in the MLPs tend to be more focused on encoding similar types of knowledge. We experimentally validate that this specialized distribution of knowledge contributes to improving the efficiency of knowledge utilization in these models. Furthermore, by conducting causal training experiments, we confirm that this specialized knowledge distribution plays a critical role in improving the model's efficiency in leveraging stored knowledge.

papers.title: Characterizing Learning Curves During Language Model Pre-Training: Learning, Forgetting, and Stability
papers.research_question: How do language models learn to make predictions during pre-training, and what features influence individual learning curves?
papers.core_contribution: The paper characterizes language model learning curves during pre-training, showing that models learn n-grams sequentially, with frequent tokens acquired earlier and more stably, and introduces metrics to quantify learning speed, forgetting, and stability.
papers.conclusion: The work identifies learning patterns and features that predict when and how stably examples are acquired, proposing a characterization based on distributional statistics.
papers.key_findings:
Models generate short repetitive phrases early in pre-training before learning to generate longer coherent text.
Learning follows n-gram stages, with models overfitting to unigrams then bigrams, etc.
Frequent tokens have lower final surprisal, are learned earlier, and exhibit less variability.
Higher n-gram probabilities correlate with lower forgettability and variability.
Longer contexts correlate with higher variability and later acquisition.
papers.limitation:
surprisal is an imperfect proxy for language model learning
only consider language models with 124M parameters trained on 5.1B tokens
future_direction: Further research on the effects of model size on learning speed, variability, and forgetting.
Characterizing examples that fluctuate at different points during pre-training across model sizes.
papers.abstract: How do language models learn to make predictions during pre-training? To study this, we extract learning curves from five autoregressive English language model pre-training runs, for 1M unseen tokens in context. We observe that the language models generate short repetitive phrases before learning to generate longer and more coherent text. We also find that individual tokens often exhibit sudden increases or decreases in loss that are surprisingly consistent across pre-training runs. To better understand these fluctuations, we quantify the final surprisal, within-run variability, age of acquisition, forgettability, and cross-run variability of learning curves for individual tokens in context. More frequent tokens reach lower final surprisals, exhibit less variability within and across pre-training runs, are learned earlier, and are less likely to be "forgotten" during pre-training. Higher n-gram probabilities further accentuate these effects. Independent of the target token, shorter and more frequent contexts correlate with marginally more stable and quickly acquired predictions. Based on our results, we argue for the existence of sequential learning dependencies between different model capabilities, and we characterize language model learning as early n-gram learning before gradual refinement of tail n-gram predictions.

papers.title: Probing Representation Forgetting in Supervised and Unsupervised Continual Learning
papers.research_question: How does representation forgetting, measured by linear probes, compare to catastrophic forgetting measured by observed accuracy in continual learning? What are the implications for understanding and designing continual learning methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that representation forgetting, measured by linear probes, is often less severe than catastrophic forgetting measured by observed accuracy, and that simple fine-tuning with contrastive losses can be competitive with specialized continual learning methods, especially in longer task sequences.
papers.conclusion: Evaluating representations via linear probes provides new insights into continual learning, showing that representation forgetting is less severe than previously thought, and that simple methods like supervised contrastive learning with prototype-based classification are promising.
papers.key_findings:
Representation forgetting measured by linear probes is often small for naive fine-tuning, challenging the notion of catastrophic forgetting.
Supervised contrastive learning (SupCon) and SimCLR exhibit less representation forgetting and can even show positive backward transfer.
Increasing model width reduces representation forgetting more than depth, which is not apparent from observed accuracy.
Linear probe evaluation reveals that representation forgetting is concentrated in higher layers of the network.
A simple method using SupCon and nearest mean of exemplars (NME) achieves competitive performance without needing a replay buffer during training.
papers.limitation:
Linear probe performance may not be the only criteria to fully evaluate knowledge retention from past tasks.
The work focuses on the task-incremental setting and does not consider the class-incremental setting.
Results over more distant tasks (e.g., ImageNet to sketch images) may be needed to fully understand representation forgetting.
future_direction: Extend the study to class-incremental setting.
Evaluate on more distant tasks, such as ImageNet to sketch images.
papers.abstract: Continual Learning research typically focuses on tackling the phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting in neural networks. Catastrophic forgetting is associated with an abrupt loss of knowledge previously learned by a model when the task, or more broadly the data distribution, being trained on changes. In supervised learning problems this forgetting, resulting from a change in the model's representation, is typically measured or observed by evaluating the decrease in old task performance. However, a model's representation can change without losing knowledge about prior tasks. In this work we consider the concept of representation forgetting, observed by using the difference in performance of an optimal linear classifier before and after a new task is introduced. Using this tool we revisit a number of standard continual learning benchmarks and observe that, through this lens, model representations trained without any explicit control for forgetting often experience small representation forgetting and can sometimes be comparable to methods which explicitly control for forgetting, especially in longer task sequences. We also show that representation forgetting can lead to new insights on the effect of model capacity and loss function used in continual learning. Based on our results, we show that a simple yet competitive approach is to learn representations continually with standard supervised contrastive learning while constructing prototypes of class samples when queried on old samples.

papers.title: Fine-tuning can cripple your foundation model; preserving features may be the solution
papers.research_question: How does end-to-end fine-tuning of a foundation model affect its pre-trained knowledge, and can we reduce the resulting concept forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a new fine-tuning regularizer (LDIFS) that minimizes the ℓ2 distance in feature space between the pre-trained and fine-tuned models, significantly reducing concept forgetting while maintaining downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: Concept forgetting is a significant undesirable side effect of fine-tuning foundation models, and the proposed LDIFS method provides an effective solution by preserving pre-trained features during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
End-to-end fine-tuning of foundation models causes significant 'concept forgetting', where the model loses its ability to recognize concepts outside the downstream task.
Regularizing the fine-tuned model to stay close to the pre-trained model in parameter space (L2SP) helps reduce concept forgetting, but regularizing in feature space is more effective.
The proposed LDIFS method, which preserves features from multiple internal representations, outperforms existing fine-tuning methods in minimizing concept forgetting without harming downstream task accuracy.
LDIFS is also effective in a continual fine-tuning setup, outperforming both standard fine-tuning and classic continual learning baselines in preserving and accumulating knowledge across a sequence of tasks.
Preserving only the last-layer features is not effective; preserving features from different internal representations is crucial for reducing concept forgetting.
papers.limitation:
LDIFS has a hyperparameter λ that requires cross-validation, and the cross-validated value may not always yield the best model for concept forgetting or downstream performance.
The paper uses a fixed set of evenly spaced features; an analysis of which features are useful for encoding which concepts is an open question.
If the pre-trained model contains biases and undesirable behaviors, LDIFS may preserve them in the fine-tuned model.
The study is limited to CLIP and image classification tasks; understanding concept forgetting in other foundation model families (e.g., LLMs) is left for future work.
future_direction: Investigating better ways to set the LDIFS hyperparameter λ.
Analyzing which features are useful for encoding which concepts.
Studying how to prevent undesirable behaviors (e.g., biases) from being distilled into the fine-tuned model while preserving pre-trained knowledge.
Extending the study of concept forgetting to other foundation model families such as Large Language Models.
Fundamentally defining what a 'concept' is and the granularity at which we should study it for foundation models.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained foundation models, due to their enormous capacity and exposure to vast amounts of data during pre-training, are known to have learned plenty of real-world concepts. An important step in making these pre-trained models effective on downstream tasks is to fine-tune them on related datasets. While various fine-tuning methods have been devised and have been shown to be highly effective, we observe that a fine-tuned model's ability to recognize concepts on tasks $\textit{different}$ from the downstream one is reduced significantly compared to its pre-trained counterpart. This is an undesirable effect of fine-tuning as a substantial amount of resources was used to learn these pre-trained concepts in the first place. We call this phenomenon ''concept forgetting'' and via experiments show that most end-to-end fine-tuning approaches suffer heavily from this side effect. To this end, we propose a simple fix to this problem by designing a new fine-tuning method called $\textit{LDIFS}$ (short for $\ell_2$ distance in feature space) that, while learning new concepts related to the downstream task, allows a model to preserve its pre-trained knowledge as well. Through extensive experiments on 10 fine-tuning tasks we show that $\textit{LDIFS}$ significantly reduces concept forgetting. Additionally, we show that LDIFS is highly effective in performing continual fine-tuning on a sequence of tasks as well, in comparison with both fine-tuning as well as continual learning baselines.

papers.title: Detecting Memorization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can memorization in large language models be detected with high precision and interpretability by analyzing internal neuron activations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method that uses neuron activations to detect memorization with near-perfect accuracy and enables intervention to suppress memorization without degrading overall model performance.
papers.conclusion: The method provides precise detection and intervention for memorization, enhancing model interpretability and evaluation integrity by ensuring metrics reflect generalization rather than recall.
papers.key_findings:
Individual neuron activations, especially in MLP layers, can separate memorized and not memorized tokens with up to 99% accuracy.
Trained linear and two-layer probes achieve 99.9% accuracy in detecting memorization.
The same methodology can be applied to detect repetition with similarly high accuracy.
Intervening on identified activation patterns can suppress memorization and repetition mechanisms without harming the model's overall predictive ability.
The model encodes a certainty mechanism, reflected in activation 1668, which correlates with high-confidence predictions like those in memorization and repetition.
papers.limitation:
The trained probes are specific to the model architecture and dataset used; applying them to other models or datasets may require adjustments.
The method is primarily effective for verbatim memorization; detecting more nuanced forms (e.g., format-based or knowledge memorization) may be challenging.
The probes might capture additional internal processes beyond just memorization or repetition, requiring further research to disentangle.
future_direction: Apply the methodology to other mechanisms such as factual retrieval, logical reasoning, and mathematics.
Use token labeling based on internal representations for specialized training of LLMs for specific use cases.
Develop uncertainty-aware inference methods leveraging the identified certainty mechanism.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved impressive results in natural language processing but are prone to memorizing portions of their training data, which can compromise evaluation metrics, raise privacy concerns, and limit generalization. Traditional methods for detecting memorization rely on output probabilities or loss functions, often lacking precision due to confounding factors like common language patterns. In this paper, we introduce an analytical method that precisely detects memorization by examining neuron activations within the LLM. By identifying specific activation patterns that differentiate between memorized and not memorized tokens, we train classification probes that achieve near-perfect accuracy. The approach can also be applied to other mechanisms, such as repetition, as demonstrated in this study, highlighting its versatility. Intervening on these activations allows us to suppress memorization without degrading overall performance, enhancing evaluation integrity by ensuring metrics reflect genuine generalization. Additionally, our method supports large-scale labeling of tokens and sequences, crucial for next-generation AI models, improving training efficiency and results. Our findings contribute to model interpretability and offer practical tools for analyzing and controlling internal mechanisms in LLMs.

papers.title: RECALL: REpresentation-aligned Catastrophic-forgetting ALLeviation via Hierarchical Model Merging
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate catastrophic forgetting in large language models without access to historical data, by leveraging internal representations for model merging?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes RECALL, a representation-aware model merging framework that uses layer-wise hidden representation similarities to align and merge models, mitigating catastrophic forgetting without needing historical data.
papers.conclusion: RECALL provides an effective, data-free solution for continual learning in LLMs by aligning representations during model merging, mitigating catastrophic forgetting and enabling multi-domain knowledge fusion.
papers.key_findings:
RECALL outperforms baselines in knowledge retention and generalization across five NLP tasks.
RECALL effectively fuses knowledge from multiple fine-tuned models without access to historical data.
RECALL maintains stable performance in sequential fine-tuning, showing strong resistance to catastrophic forgetting.
Representation similarity (using RBF kernel) is an effective guide for layer-wise model merging.
RECALL works with both single and multiple model merging, and with or without the base model.
papers.limitation:
Assumes access to multiple fine-tuned models on related tasks, which may not always be available.
Relies on clustering and similarity computations over a small set of representative samples, which can influence merging outcome.
Tailored to models with identical architectures and aligned tokenizers; extending to heterogeneous models or multilingual settings is challenging.
Scaling to dozens of tasks or integrating with training-time regularization techniques needs further investigation.
future_direction: Extending RECALL to heterogeneous model families or multilingual settings.
Scaling RECALL to dozens of tasks.
Integrating RECALL with training-time regularization techniques for tighter lifelong learning integration.
papers.abstract: We unveil that internal representations in large language models (LLMs) serve as reliable proxies of learned knowledge, and propose RECALL, a novel representation-aware model merging framework for continual learning without access to historical data. RECALL computes inter-model similarity from layer-wise hidden representations over clustered typical samples, and performs adaptive, hierarchical parameter fusion to align knowledge across models. This design enables the preservation of domain-general features in shallow layers while allowing task-specific adaptation in deeper layers. Unlike prior methods that require task labels or incur performance trade-offs, RECALL achieves seamless multi-domain integration and strong resistance to catastrophic forgetting. Extensive experiments across five NLP tasks and multiple continual learning scenarios show that RECALL outperforms baselines in both knowledge retention and generalization, providing a scalable and data-free solution for evolving LLMs.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: The mosaic memory of large language models
papers.research_question: Do large language models memorize training data only through exact repetitions, or do they assemble information from similar sequences (fuzzy duplicates)?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models exhibit mosaic memory, memorizing sequences through exposure to fuzzy duplicates, and this memorization is predominantly syntactic rather than semantic.
papers.conclusion: Mosaic memory reveals that LLM memorization is a complex process involving fuzzy duplicates, challenging current assumptions and practices in deduplication, privacy protection, and benchmarking.
papers.key_findings:
