Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Repetitions are not all alike: distinct mechanisms sustain repetition in language models
papers.research_question: What are the distinct underlying mechanisms that sustain repetition in language models, and how do they develop during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that repetition in language models arises from two distinct mechanisms: a learned, circuit-based mechanism for in-context learning-induced repetition and an early-emerging, fallback mechanism for natural repetition.
papers.conclusion: Repetition in language models stems from two distinct mechanisms: a learned, circuit-based mechanism for ICL-induced repetition and an early-emerging fallback mechanism for natural repetition, which arises when the model fails to attend to informative tokens.
papers.key_findings:
ICL-induced repetition develops progressively over training, while natural repetition emerges early and persists.
ICL repetition relies on a dedicated circuit of attention heads that specialize over training, while natural repetition does not show such circuitry.
Attention during natural repetition focuses disproportionately on low-information tokens (like newlines), suggesting a fallback behavior.
MLP contributions to repetition are strong in ICL but weak in natural repetition.
ICL repetition leads to lower entropy (higher confidence) as cycles increase, while natural repetition shows higher uncertainty.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to Pythia, a relatively small-scale model, and may not generalize to other models or architectures.
future_direction: Extend analysis to models of varying sizes and architectures.
Investigate the causal mechanisms behind early-emerging repetition patterns.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can sometimes degrade into repetitive loops, persistently generating identical word sequences. Because repetition is rare in natural human language, its frequent occurrence across diverse tasks and contexts in LLMs remains puzzling. Here we investigate whether behaviorally similar repetition patterns arise from distinct underlying mechanisms and how these mechanisms develop during model training. We contrast two conditions: repetitions elicited by natural text prompts with those induced by in-context learning (ICL) setups that explicitly require copying behavior. Our analyses reveal that ICL-induced repetition relies on a dedicated network of attention heads that progressively specialize over training, whereas naturally occurring repetition emerges early and lacks a defined circuitry. Attention inspection further shows that natural repetition focuses disproportionately on low-information tokens, suggesting a fallback behavior when relevant context cannot be retrieved. These results indicate that superficially similar repetition behaviors originate from qualitatively different internal processes, reflecting distinct modes of failure and adaptation in language models.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: Calibrating Factual Knowledge in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in Pretrained Language Models without re-training from scratch?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CALINET, a lightweight method to calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs by adding and training new parameters (calibration memory slots) while freezing the original model, effectively reducing false knowledge and generalizing to downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper reassesses knowledge in PLMs with CKA, proposes CALINET to calibrate knowledge at scale without updating original parameters, and shows it generalizes well to downstream tasks, with neuron-level investigations into the calibration mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive Knowledge Assessment (CKA) reveals that nearly 50% of facts are stored incorrectly in PLMs.
CALINET effectively calibrates false facts, reducing the False Rate from 48.10% to 17.09% for T5-base on 100 facts.
CALINET generalizes calibrated knowledge to downstream question answering tasks, improving performance on calibration subsets without harming performance on other questions.
Analysis shows that calibration memory slots are more knowledge-intensive than original FFN values, with nearly 80% corresponding to meaningful concepts.
CALINET adjusts the output token distribution to increase the probability of the correct fact and its synonyms, indicating generalized calibration.
papers.limitation:
Relies on existing knowledge bases and synthetic data for assessment and calibration, which may not fully capture real-world knowledge complexity.
Evaluates PLMs via their predictions, which is a biased approach and may not accurately assess factual knowledge correctness.
Cannot completely calibrate all factual errors in PLMs.
future_direction: Improve calibration applicability in reality by moving beyond synthetic data.
Develop more accurate methods for assessing factual knowledge correctness in PLMs.
Develop more advanced knowledge calibration methods.
papers.abstract: Previous literature has proved that Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) can store factual knowledge. However, we find that facts stored in the PLMs are not always correct. It motivates us to explore a fundamental question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs without re-training from scratch? In this work, we propose a simple and lightweight method CaliNet to achieve this goal. To be specific, we first detect whether PLMs can learn the right facts via a contrastive score between right and fake facts. If not, we then use a lightweight method to add and adapt new parameters to specific factual texts. Experiments on the knowledge probing task show the calibration effectiveness and efficiency. In addition, through closed-book question answering, we find that the calibrated PLM possesses knowledge generalization ability after finetuning.Beyond the calibration performance, we further investigate and visualize the knowledge calibration mechanism.

papers.title: Functional Abstraction of Knowledge Recall in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the knowledge recall mechanism in large language models be abstracted into a functional structure, and how can this perspective be used to improve knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a functional abstraction of knowledge recall in LLMs, showing that hidden activation vectors correspond to independent functional components (input, function body, return value). This perspective is used to improve contextual knowledge editing via activation patching.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge recall process in LLMs can be abstracted as a functional structure with localized activation vectors serving as independent components, and this abstraction enables more effective knowledge editing through activation patching.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge-aware activation vectors are localized to specific token positions and layers: subject and relation vectors in early layers within their token ranges, object vectors in late layers at the final token.
These localized activation vectors function as independent components (input argument, function body, return value) in the knowledge recall process.
Activation interchange experiments show that subject, relation, and object vectors can be swapped independently, supporting the functional abstraction.
The proposed knowledge-scoring algorithm based on activation patching can accurately identify these functional components.
Applying this functional perspective via activation patching improves the efficacy of contextual knowledge editing prompts.
papers.limitation:
The proposed knowledge scoring algorithm relies on a brute-force search method, resulting in high time complexity.
The framework awaits validation on text-generation and general question-answering tasks that specifically involve knowledge recall.
The accuracy of the proposed knowledge editing method requires improvement, suggesting representation rewriting does not fully encapsulate the original knowledge.
future_direction: Developing more efficient knowledge exploration algorithms.
Validating the framework on text-generation and general question-answering tasks.
Deeper exploration of the knowledge storage mechanisms within LLMs.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained transformer large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong knowledge recall capabilities. This paper investigates the knowledge recall mechanism in LLMs by abstracting it into a functional structure. We propose that during knowledge recall, the model's hidden activation space implicitly entails a function execution process where specific activation vectors align with functional components (Input argument, Function body, and Return values). Specifically, activation vectors of relation-related tokens define a mapping function from subjects to objects, with subject-related token activations serving as input arguments and object-related token activations as return values. For experimental verification, we first design a patching-based knowledge-scoring algorithm to identify knowledge-aware activation vectors as independent functional components. Then, we conduct counter-knowledge testing to examine the independent functional effects of each component on knowledge recall outcomes. From this functional perspective, we improve the contextual knowledge editing approach augmented by activation patching. By rewriting incoherent activations in context, we enable improved short-term memory retention for new knowledge prompting.

papers.title: Unveiling and Addressing Pseudo Forgetting in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does performance degradation in continual learning stem from a loss of capabilities or from failure to activate them? The paper argues it is the latter, termed pseudo forgetting.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies pseudo forgetting in continual learning of LLMs, where performance drops due to failure to activate capabilities rather than loss of them, and proposes RGD-R, a replay-based method that dynamically allocates data based on a new metric called RGD.
papers.conclusion: The paper directly demonstrates pseudo forgetting in LLMs during continual learning, introduces the RGD score to quantify it, and proposes RGD-R which dynamically allocates replay data to address pseudo forgetting and preserve plasticity.
papers.key_findings:
Pseudo forgetting exists: performance degradation on previous tasks is not due to loss of capabilities but failure of instructions to activate them.
Providing partial correct rationale or task-irrelevant suffixes can restore performance to pre-forgetting levels.
Pseudo forgetting is caused by reduced instruction dependence during rationale generation.
The proposed Rationale-Guidance Difficulty (RGD) metric can measure the difficulty of activating correct capabilities.
The RGD-R framework effectively mitigates pseudo forgetting while maintaining model plasticity.
papers.limitation:
No in-depth analysis of the specific process behind pseudo forgetting (e.g., when during learning the dependence declines).
The relationship between pseudo forgetting and specific tasks or domains remains unexplored.
RGD score is one possible metric; developing more comprehensive evaluation metrics requires additional research.
future_direction: Combine replay-based and parameter-based approaches for continual learning.
Develop more comprehensive evaluation metrics for pseudo forgetting.
Enhance asynchronous knowledge transfer capabilities.
papers.abstract: Although substantial efforts have been made to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in continual learning, the intrinsic mechanisms are not well understood.In this work, we demonstrate the existence of "pseudo forgetting": the performance degradation on previous tasks is not attributed to a loss of capabilities, but rather to the failure of the instructions to activate the appropriate model abilities.We show that the model's performance on previous tasks can be restored through two simple interventions: (1) providing partial external correct rationale, and (2) appending semantically meaningless suffixes to the original instructions, to guide the generation of correct rationales.Through empirical analysis of the internal mechanisms governing rationale generation, we reveal that models exhibiting pseudo forgetting show reduced instruction dependence during rationale generation, leading to suboptimal activation of their inherent capabilities.Based on this insight, we propose Rationale-Guidance Difficulty based Replay (RGD-R) framework that dynamically allocates replay data based on the model's ability to correctly leverage the intrinsic capabilities.Experimental results demonstrate that RGD-R effectively mitigates pseudo forgetting while maintaining model plasticity.

papers.title: On robustness of generative representations against catastrophic forgetting
papers.research_question: What is the root cause of catastrophic forgetting in neural networks, and how do generative representations compare to discriminative ones in terms of robustness against forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Generative representations learned by autoencoders and variational autoencoders are more robust to catastrophic forgetting and more transferable than discriminative representations, highlighting advantages for continual learning.
papers.conclusion: Generative representations are more robust and transferable, suggesting new research directions for adopting generative models in continual learning beyond replay mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Generative representations are less prone to catastrophic forgetting compared to discriminative ones, as shown by stable accuracy and CKA similarity.
Generative models learn more transferable features, enabling good performance on future tasks without retraining.
Forgetting in generative models is gradual and monotonic, unlike the chaotic forgetting in discriminative models.
High accuracy (over 90%) can be achieved on continual learning benchmarks without dedicated anti-forgetting mechanisms.
The lack of catastrophic forgetting in reconstruction tasks is due to the generality of features learned by generative models.
papers.limitation:
Generative representations can have poor discriminative abilities, which may limit the informativeness of accuracy-based measures.
Current proxy tasks like classification may hinder precise analysis of catastrophic forgetting.
future_direction: Develop task-agnostic measures of catastrophic forgetting.
Use generative learning mechanisms to obtain better representations for discrimination tasks in continual learning.
Investigate if the generic nature of generative representations is the sole explanation for lack of catastrophic forgetting.
papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting of previously learned knowledge while learning new tasks is a widely observed limitation of contemporary neural networks. Although many continual learning methods are proposed to mitigate this drawback, the main question remains unanswered: what is the root cause of catastrophic forgetting? In this work, we aim at answering this question by posing and validating a set of research hypotheses related to the specificity of representations built internally by neural models. More specifically, we design a set of empirical evaluations that compare the robustness of representations in discriminative and generative models against catastrophic forgetting. We observe that representations learned by discriminative models are more prone to catastrophic forgetting than their generative counterparts, which sheds new light on the advantages of developing generative models for continual learning. Finally, our work opens new research pathways and possibilities to adopt generative models in continual learning beyond mere replay mechanisms.

papers.title: Are formal and functional linguistic mechanisms dissociated in language models?
papers.research_question: Do current large language models exhibit distinct localization (dissociation) of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms in their internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence for formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness (formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than functional ones, and vice-versa), but not in terms of circuit overlap, suggesting a shared pool of mechanisms for formal tasks rather than a single unified region.
papers.conclusion: There is evidence for emerging formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness, but not in terms of circuit overlap, indicating a set of shared formal linguistic mechanisms rather than a single unified region.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for formal and functional linguistic tasks have low overlap (IoU).
Circuits for formal tasks do not have especially high overlap with each other, arguing against a single unified formal network.
Formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than they perform functional tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Functional task circuits perform other functional tasks better than they perform formal tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Clustering based on cross-task faithfulness vectors separates formal and functional tasks into distinct groups.
papers.limitation: The circuit-finding method (EAP-IG) may not perfectly capture all relevant mechanisms, and the findings are limited to the specific models and tasks studied.
future_direction: Studying more models and tasks to generalize findings.
Using more granular analyses (e.g., neuron-level, sparse feature circuits).
Investigating the effects of model scale and architecture on dissociation.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, these capabilities are unevenly distributed: they excel at formal linguistic tasks, such as producing fluent, grammatical text, but struggle more with functional linguistic tasks like reasoning and consistent fact retrieval. Inspired by neuroscience, recent work suggests that to succeed on both formal and functional linguistic tasks, LLMs should use different mechanisms for each; such localization could either be built-in or emerge spontaneously through training. In this paper, we ask: do current models, with fast-improving functional linguistic abilities, exhibit distinct localization of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms? We answer this by finding and comparing the "circuits", or minimal computational subgraphs, responsible for various formal and functional tasks. Comparing 5 LLMs across 10 distinct tasks, we find that while there is indeed little overlap between circuits for formal and functional tasks, there is also little overlap between formal linguistic tasks, as exists in the human brain. Thus, a single formal linguistic network, unified and distinct from functional task circuits, remains elusive. However, in terms of cross-task faithfulness - the ability of one circuit to solve another's task - we observe a separation between formal and functional mechanisms, suggesting that shared mechanisms between formal tasks may exist.

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
papers.conclusion: Concept editing is a challenging task for LLMs, and existing editing methods have limitations in modifying conceptual knowledge without distorting related instances. This work provides a benchmark and metrics to inspire further research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) can achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions in LLMs.
These methods perform poorly on concept-specific metrics like Instance Change and Concept Consistency, indicating they distort related instance knowledge.
There is a gap between reliability (token-level accuracy) and concept consistency (semantic similarity of generated definitions).
Concept editing is easier when the replacement definition comes from the same superclass (intra module) compared to a different superclass (inter module).
Causal tracing reveals that conceptual knowledge is stored differently from instance knowledge, with attention mechanisms in earlier layers playing a key role.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are limited to models up to 7B parameters; larger models may exhibit different behaviors.
The generalization of edited concepts to unseen instances or related concepts is not fully explored.
The mechanisms of how LLMs learn and represent concepts and concept hierarchies are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring concept editing in larger-scale language models.
Improving the generalization of edited concepts to related knowledge.
Studying the mechanisms of concept learning and representation in LLMs.

papers.title: Emergent effects of scaling on the functional hierarchies within large language models
papers.research_question: What is the functional hierarchy of abstraction across layers in LLMs, and how does it change with model scaling?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models exhibit functional hierarchies with abstraction increasing across layers, but scaling introduces deviations such as double representation peaks and anti-persistent fluctuations in attention mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms functional hierarchies in LLMs but reveals emergent deviations with scaling, such as double representation peaks and layer coordination, complicating interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Item-level semantics are most strongly represented in early layers (2-7), two-item relations in middle layers (8-12), and four-item analogies in later layers (10-15), consistent with an abstraction hierarchy.
Deep layers can represent narrow two-item relations from early in the context, suggesting information compression without meaningful abstraction.
In the large Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct model, representation of two-item relations and analogies shows two distinct peaks (layers 12-16 and 25-33), indicating fluctuations in abstraction level.
Adjacent layers in the large model exhibit anti-persistent fluctuations in attention outputs, with negative autocorrelation, suggesting coordinated specialization.
Buried concepts (target text followed by filler) are represented in deeper layers, showing that late layers capture global document-wide information.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of the double-peak pattern and valley in large models is unclear and requires further work.
Analyses on grammar and syntax were inconclusive and not reported, limiting insights into syntactic processing.
future_direction: Study larger models to understand scaling effects further.
Investigate the mechanisms behind the double-peak representation and layer coordination.
Explore how late-layer representations can be used for steering and safety applications.
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) architectures are often described as functionally hierarchical: Early layers process syntax, middle layers begin to parse semantics, and late layers integrate information. The present work revisits these ideas. This research submits simple texts to an LLM (e.g., "A church and organ") and extracts the resulting activations. Then, for each layer, support vector machines and ridge regressions are fit to predict a text's label and thus examine whether a given layer encodes some information. Analyses using a small model (Llama-3.2-3b; 28 layers) partly bolster the common hierarchical perspective: Item-level semantics are most strongly represented early (layers 2-7), then two-item relations (layers 8-12), and then four-item analogies (layers 10-15). Afterward, the representation of items and simple relations gradually decreases in deeper layers that focus on more global information. However, several findings run counter to a steady hierarchy view: First, although deep layers can represent document-wide abstractions, deep layers also compress information from early portions of the context window without meaningful abstraction. Second, when examining a larger model (Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct), stark fluctuations in abstraction level appear: As depth increases, two-item relations and four-item analogies initially increase in their representation, then markedly decrease, and afterward increase again momentarily. This peculiar pattern consistently emerges across several experiments. Third, another emergent effect of scaling is coordination between the attention mechanisms of adjacent layers. Across multiple experiments using the larger model, adjacent layers fluctuate between what information they each specialize in representing. In sum, an abstraction hierarchy often manifests across layers, but large models also deviate from this structure in curious ways.

papers.title: Probing Linguistic Features of Sentence-Level Representations in Relation Extraction
papers.research_question: What linguistic features are captured by sentence-level representations in neural relation extraction models, and how do different encoder architectures and the inclusion of linguistic features affect the learned representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a set of 14 probing tasks specifically designed for relation extraction and uses them to analyze how encoder architectures and linguistic features bias the linguistic properties captured in sentence-level representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces probing tasks for relation extraction and shows that encoder architectures and linguistic features bias the learned representations, with self-attentive encoders capturing deeper features not fully captured by the probing tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Adding contextualized word representations (ELMo, BERT) greatly increases performance on probing tasks focusing on named entity and part-of-speech information, and yields better results in relation extraction.
Entity masking improves relation extraction performance but considerably lowers performance on entity type related probing tasks, indicating a shift in focus away from entity mentions.
Encoder architecture bias clearly affects learned properties: CNN and Bi-LSTM perform well on local probing tasks (e.g., argument distance, part-of-speech context), while GCN performs well on dependency-related tasks.
Self-attentive encoders show superior relation extraction performance but consistently perform lower on the probing tasks, suggesting they capture 'deeper' linguistic features not covered by the current probing tasks.
Probing task performance does not necessarily correlate with relation extraction performance; models that perform better on probing tasks do not always perform better on the downstream task.
papers.limitation: The probing tasks do not cover all linguistic patterns, such as appositions, and do not investigate generalization to specific entity types.
future_direction: Extend the probing tasks to cover specific linguistic patterns such as appositions.
Investigate a model's ability of generalizing to specific entity types, e.g., company and person names.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent progress, little is known about the features captured by state-of-the-art neural relation extraction (RE) models. Common methods encode the source sentence, conditioned on the entity mentions, before classifying the relation. However, the complexity of the task makes it difficult to understand how encoder architecture and supporting linguistic knowledge affect the features learned by the encoder. We introduce 14 probing tasks targeting linguistic properties relevant to RE, and we use them to study representations learned by more than 40 different encoder architecture and linguistic feature combinations trained on two datasets, TACRED and SemEval 2010 Task 8. We find that the bias induced by the architecture and the inclusion of linguistic features are clearly expressed in the probing task performance. For example, adding contextualized word representations greatly increases performance on probing tasks with a focus on named entity and part-of-speech information, and yields better results in RE. In contrast, entity masking improves RE, but considerably lowers performance on entity type related probing tasks.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: Feature Forgetting in Continual Representation Learning
papers.research_question: What are the characteristics of representation learning in continual learning, and how does feature forgetting affect it?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a protocol for evaluating representation in continual learning, identifies feature forgetting as a key deficiency, and proposes gating adapters to mitigate feature forgetting, thereby improving representation learning.
papers.conclusion: Representation learning and catastrophic forgetting are largely separate issues in continual learning, and improving representation learning benefits both old and new tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Representation learning in continual learning is consistently deficient compared to multi-task learning, and the gap increases with the number of tasks.
Feature forgetting is a prevalent problem in continual learning, where previously learned features are erased and have to be re-learned.
Common techniques for mitigating catastrophic forgetting (e.g., regularization, replay) have little effect on improving representation learning.
Gating adapters, which selectively activate units based on task features, can mitigate feature forgetting and improve representation learning.
Improving representation learning can also improve average accuracy on past tasks when combined with rehearsal methods.
papers.limitation:
The study investigates feature forgetting, which is only one of the limiting factors of representation learning; other factors like gradient noise and negative transfer are not addressed.
The study does not cover other representation modalities such as text or other models such as Transformers.
future_direction: Further investigation on the representation learning component of continual and lifelong learning.
Expanding the discussion to other representation modalities such as text and other models such as Transformers.
Studying the combination of adapters with conventional forgetting-mitigation methods such as replay.
papers.abstract: In continual and lifelong learning, good representation learning can help increase performance and reduce sample complexity when learning new tasks. There is evidence that representations do not suffer from "catastrophic forgetting" even in plain continual learning, but little further fact is known about its characteristics. In this paper, we aim to gain more understanding about representation learning in continual learning, especially on the feature forgetting problem. We devise a protocol for evaluating representation in continual learning, and then use it to present an overview of the basic trends of continual representation learning, showing its consistent deficiency and potential issues. To study the feature forgetting problem, we create a synthetic dataset to identify and visualize the prevalence of feature forgetting in neural networks. Finally, we propose a simple technique using gating adapters to mitigate feature forgetting. We conclude by discussing that improving representation learning benefits both old and new tasks in continual learning.

papers.title: Putting a Face to Forgetting: Continual Learning meets Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can catastrophic forgetting in continual learning be understood at a mechanistic level in terms of transformations to individual features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mechanistic framework that interprets catastrophic forgetting in continual learning as rotations and scalings of feature vectors, leading to capacity degradation and readout misalignment.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a new vocabulary for diagnosing continual learning failures and shows that fading and misalignment are key drivers of forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
Forgetting is driven by rotations and scalings of feature vectors, which reduce allocated capacity and cause readout misalignment.
Worst-case forgetting occurs when tasks share features but with misaligned probes, leading to overlap and fading.
Depth worsens forgetting by increasing fading and overlap.
In a practical Vision Transformer, forgetting is driven more by fading and readout misalignment than by overlap.
Crosscoders can be used to track feature evolution in continual learning.
papers.limitation:
The tractable model assumes fixed probes, which exaggerates forgetting.
Crosscoder features are approximations and not ground-truth.
future_direction: Formal analysis of the effect of depth on feature norms and rotations.
Leveraging faded late-layer features identified at earlier layers to mitigate forgetting.
papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting in continual learning is often measured at the performance or last-layer representation level, overlooking the underlying mechanisms. We introduce a mechanistic framework that offers a geometric interpretation of catastrophic forgetting as the result of transformations to the encoding of individual features. These transformations can lead to forgetting by reducing the allocated capacity of features (worse representation) and disrupting their readout by downstream computations. Analysis of a tractable model formalizes this view, allowing us to identify best- and worst-case scenarios. Through experiments on this model, we empirically test our formal analysis and highlight the detrimental effect of depth. Finally, we demonstrate how our framework can be used in the analysis of practical models through the use of Crosscoders. We present a case study of a Vision Transformer trained on sequential CIFAR-10. Our work provides a new, feature-centric vocabulary for continual learning.

papers.title: Pierce the Mists, Greet the Sky: Decipher Knowledge Overshadowing via Knowledge Circuit Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the origins and internal mechanisms of knowledge overshadowing in large language models during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PHANTOMCIRCUIT, a framework that uses knowledge circuit analysis to dissect the internal mechanisms and training dynamics of knowledge overshadowing in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: PHANTOMCIRCUIT effectively analyzes and detects knowledge overshadowing, offering insights into its mechanisms and a pathway for recovery via circuit optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Higher knowledge popularity (P) and model size (M) cause earlier onset, shorter duration, and quicker recovery from knowledge overshadowing.
Larger dataset size (D) leads to earlier onset but slower recovery from overshadowing.
Knowledge overshadowing dynamics are driven by the co-evolution of subordinate knowledge loss proportion (LP) and relative overshadowing rate (RO).
Attention heads in knowledge circuits that focus on {Xdom, Xsub} are crucial for mitigating overshadowing.
Optimizing the number of edges in knowledge circuits can recover from overshadowing by enhancing attention on key differences.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily rely on synthetic data for controlled analysis, limiting generalization to real-world data.
Applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation is not yet validated.
Dynamic analysis of knowledge circuits throughout training is computationally intensive, hindering scalability.
future_direction: Validate the conclusions on more complex, noisy real-world data and other model architectures.
Explore applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation.
Develop more computationally efficient circuit analysis techniques, such as Information Flow Routes (IFR).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their remarkable capabilities, are hampered by hallucinations. A particularly challenging variant, knowledge overshadowing, occurs when one piece of activated knowledge inadvertently masks another relevant piece, leading to erroneous outputs even with high-quality training data. Current understanding of overshadowing is largely confined to inference-time observations, lacking deep insights into its origins and internal mechanisms during model training. Therefore, we introduce PhantomCircuit, a novel framework designed to comprehensively analyze and detect knowledge overshadowing. By innovatively employing knowledge circuit analysis, PhantomCircuit dissects the function of key components in the circuit and how the attention pattern dynamics contribute to the overshadowing phenomenon and its evolution throughout the training process. Extensive experiments demonstrate PhantomCircuit's effectiveness in identifying such instances, offering novel insights into this elusive hallucination and providing the research community with a new methodological lens for its potential mitigation.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Subspace Chronicles: How Linguistic Information Emerges, Shifts and Interacts during Language Model Training
papers.research_question: How and when during language model training do different types of linguistic information (syntax, semantics, reasoning) emerge, shift, and interact?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an information-theoretic probing suite to extract and compare task-specific representational subspaces, revealing critical learning phases during LM training where linguistic information emerges, shares information, and later disentangles to specialize.
papers.conclusion: The subspace-based approach provides deeper insights into LM learning dynamics, showing that linguistic information continues to change even after performance stabilizes, and that cross-task similarities follow linguistic intuitions, with implications for interpretability, multi-task learning, and learning from limited data.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic knowledge is acquired rapidly after 0.5% of full training.
Continued performance improvements primarily stem from acquisition of open-domain knowledge, while semantics and reasoning tasks benefit from later boosts to long-range contextualization and higher specialization.
Cross-task similarity reveals that linguistically related tasks share information throughout training, and do so more during the critical phase of learning than before or after.
Representational subspaces continue to shift even after performance plateaus, indicating ongoing refinement of linguistic information.
The layer depth at which task information is most salient (center of gravity) changes over time, with tasks specializing to different layers later in training.
papers.limitation:
Lack of compute and training statistics for gradient-level analysis.
Linear probes may not capture more complex information for tasks like QA and NLI.
The study is limited to BERT architecture and may not generalize to larger autoregressive LMs.
The study is correlatory and does not include targeted interventions.
future_direction: Verify whether the observed dynamics hold for larger, autoregressive LMs.
Investigate early-stage multi-task learning for better downstream performance.
Revisit training encoders for under-resourced languages given the early acquisition of linguistic information.
papers.abstract: Representational spaces learned via language modeling are fundamental to Natural Language Processing (NLP), however there has been limited understanding regarding how and when during training various types of linguistic information emerge and interact. Leveraging a novel information theoretic probing suite, which enables direct comparisons of not just task performance, but their representational subspaces, we analyze nine tasks covering syntax, semantics and reasoning, across 2M pre-training steps and five seeds. We identify critical learning phases across tasks and time, during which subspaces emerge, share information, and later disentangle to specialize. Across these phases, syntactic knowledge is acquired rapidly after 0.5% of full training. Continued performance improvements primarily stem from the acquisition of open-domain knowledge, while semantics and reasoning tasks benefit from later boosts to long-range contextualization and higher specialization. Measuring cross-task similarity further reveals that linguistically related tasks share information throughout training, and do so more during the critical phase of learning than before or after. Our findings have implications for model interpretability, multi-task learning, and learning from limited data.

papers.title: Balancing Speciality and Versatility: A Coarse to Fine Framework for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can large language models gain speciality (excel in specific tasks) through fine-tuning without catastrophically forgetting their versatility (ability to handle diverse tasks)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoFiTune, a coarse-to-fine framework that selectively tunes specific modules (FFN in mid-lower layers) and applies a fine-grained soft-mask to gradients, effectively balancing speciality and versatility in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: CoFiTune effectively balances speciality and versatility in LLMs, and the analysis provides insights into the information forwarding process within transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
The optimal configuration for balancing speciality and versatility is to tune only the FFN modules in the layer range (N*25%, N*50%].
The proposed Fine-SoftMask mechanism further mitigates catastrophic forgetting in versatility without compromising speciality.
Fine-tuning only the FFN module in the mid-to-lower layer range achieves satisfactory speciality without significantly affecting versatility.
The speciality score is highest when tuning the FFN module compared to MHA or its sub-modules.
CoFiTune outperforms baseline methods across diverse tasks and model scales, achieving over 95% versatility and 90% speciality compared to original and full SFT models on average.
papers.abstract: Aligned Large Language Models (LLMs) showcase remarkable versatility, capable of handling diverse real-world tasks. Meanwhile, aligned LLMs are also expected to exhibit speciality, excelling in specific applications. However, fine-tuning with extra data, a common practice to gain speciality, often leads to catastrophic forgetting (CF) of previously acquired versatility, hindering the model's performance across diverse tasks. In response to this challenge, we propose CoFiTune, a coarse to fine framework in an attempt to strike the balance between speciality and versatility. At the coarse-grained level, an empirical tree-search algorithm is utilized to pinpoint and update specific modules that are crucial for speciality, while keeping other parameters frozen; at the fine-grained level, a soft-masking mechanism regulates the update to the LLMs, mitigating the CF issue without harming speciality. In an overall evaluation of both speciality and versatility, CoFiTune consistently outperforms baseline methods across diverse tasks and model scales. Compared to the full-parameter SFT, CoFiTune leads to about 14% versatility improvement and marginal speciality loss on a 13B model. Lastly, based on further analysis, we provide a speculative insight into the information forwarding process in LLMs, which helps explain the effectiveness of the proposed method. The code is available at https://github.com/rattlesnakey/CoFiTune.

papers.title: Erase at the Core: Representation Unlearning for Machine Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can we enforce machine unlearning throughout the entire network hierarchy to address superficial forgetting, where models achieve logit-level forgetting but retain substantial information in internal feature representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Erase at the Core (EC), a representation-based unlearning framework that uses multi-layer contrastive unlearning and deep supervision to enforce forgetting across intermediate network layers, effectively reducing representational similarity to the original model while preserving retain set utility.
papers.conclusion: EC addresses the problem of superficial forgetting by enforcing representation-level unlearning across multiple network layers, providing a practical step toward stronger machine unlearning in large-scale scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
EC achieves strong representation-level forgetting, significantly reducing similarity to the original model (low CKA and IDI) while maintaining reasonable retain set accuracy.
EC outperforms existing unlearning baselines across multiple benchmarks (ImageNet-1K, CIFAR-100) and architectures (ResNet-50, Swin-Tiny) in terms of a unified harmonic mean metric.
Layer-wise analysis shows EC induces greater divergence from the original model in deeper layers where class-discriminative features are encoded.
EC can be applied as a plug-in module to other unlearning methods (e.g., DUCK, COLA) to improve their representation-level forgetting.
Ablation studies confirm the importance of layer-wise cross-entropy loss and EC modules for stable optimization and effective forgetting.
papers.limitation:
Formal erasure guarantees remain an open direction; the evaluation is empirical.
Multi-layer supervision introduces additional computational overhead.
future_direction: Extending EC to more diverse architectures.
Integrating EC with additional unlearning methods.
papers.abstract: Many approximate machine unlearning methods demonstrate strong logit-level forgetting -- such as near-zero accuracy on the forget set -- yet continue to preserve substantial information within their internal feature representations. We refer to this discrepancy as superficial forgetting. Recent studies indicate that most existing unlearning approaches primarily alter the final classifier, leaving intermediate representations largely unchanged and highly similar to those of the original model. To address this limitation, we introduce the Erase at the Core (EC), a framework designed to enforce forgetting throughout the entire network hierarchy. EC integrates multi-layer contrastive unlearning on the forget set with retain set preservation through deeply supervised learning. Concretely, EC attaches auxiliary modules to intermediate layers and applies both contrastive unlearning and cross-entropy losses at each supervision point, with layer-wise weighted losses. Experimental results show that EC not only achieves effective logit-level forgetting, but also substantially reduces representational similarity to the original model across intermediate layers. Furthermore, EC is model-agnostic and can be incorporated as a plug-in module into existing unlearning methods, improving representation-level forgetting while maintaining performance on the retain set.

papers.title: Schema-learning and rebinding as mechanisms of in-context learning and emergence
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning work, and can it be explained through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable models like clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in-context learning can be achieved through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable clone-structured causal graphs, providing insights into how ICL works in large language models.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in CSCGs can explain in-context learning, offering insights for designing interpretable architectures and understanding emergence in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
CSCG achieves in-context learning on the GINC dataset, accurately retrieving latent concepts.
CSCG learns template circuits for algorithms and generalizes to novel tokens through rebinding on the LIALT dataset.
ICL performance improves with model overparameterization, suggesting emergence is related to capacity.
CSCG can inductively learn new word usage from single examples in the dax test.
The mechanisms of schema-learning and rebinding in CSCGs provide a plausible explanation for ICL in transformers.
papers.limitation:
CSCG fails to generalize to concepts unseen during training, similar to transformers.
Imperfections in learned CSCG models can lead to failure cases, such as wrong schema retrieval.
future_direction: Designing novel architectures based on schema-learning and rebinding principles.
Searching for interpretable and editable circuits in transformers using the identified mechanisms.
Extending the approach to more complex tasks and datasets.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is one of the most powerful and most unexpected capabilities to emerge in recent transformer-based large language models (LLMs). Yet the mechanisms that underlie it are poorly understood. In this paper, we demonstrate that comparable ICL capabilities can be acquired by an alternative sequence prediction learning method using clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs). Moreover, a key property of CSCGs is that, unlike transformer-based LLMs, they are {\em interpretable}, which considerably simplifies the task of explaining how ICL works. Specifically, we show that it uses a combination of (a) learning template (schema) circuits for pattern completion, (b) retrieving relevant templates in a context-sensitive manner, and (c) rebinding of novel tokens to appropriate slots in the templates. We go on to marshall evidence for the hypothesis that similar mechanisms underlie ICL in LLMs. For example, we find that, with CSCGs as with LLMs, different capabilities emerge at different levels of overparameterization, suggesting that overparameterization helps in learning more complex template (schema) circuits. By showing how ICL can be achieved with small models and datasets, we open up a path to novel architectures, and take a vital step towards a more general understanding of the mechanics behind this important capability.

papers.title: Hierarchical Sparse Circuit Extraction from Billion-Parameter Language Models through Scalable Attribution Graph Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can sparse computational circuits be efficiently extracted from billion-parameter language models using hierarchical decomposition and attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD), a framework that reduces circuit discovery complexity from exponential to polynomial, enabling extraction of interpretable circuits from billion-parameter models with high behavioral preservation.
papers.conclusion: HAGD enables circuit extraction from large models with preserved behavior, but limitations include incomplete attention modeling, reconstruction residuals, and interpretability challenges for large circuits.
papers.key_findings:
HAGD reduces circuit discovery complexity to O(n^2 log n) and extracts circuits from models up to 70B parameters.
Behavioral preservation ranges from 82% to 97% on algorithmic tasks and 74% to 88% on natural language benchmarks.
Cross-architecture transfer shows 52%-82% structural similarity, indicating shared computational patterns.
Circuit size grows sublinearly with model parameters, but natural language tasks yield larger, less modular circuits.
The method outperforms baselines like ACDC in scalability while maintaining comparable circuit quality.
papers.limitation:
Attention circuits are not modeled, leaving significant computational pathways unanalyzed.
Reconstruction dark matter of 15-20% unexplained variance means extracted circuits are incomplete.
Validation circularity arises from using ablation experiments that assume circuit completeness.
GNN meta-model requires ground-truth circuit labels that are expensive to obtain.
Large circuits with hundreds of nodes may exceed human interpretability limits.
future_direction: Integrate attention and MLP circuit analysis.
Characterize reconstruction residuals (dark matter).
Develop label-efficient training methods for GNN meta-model.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer neural network computations into human-understandable algorithms, yet extracting sparse computational circuits from billion-parameter language models remains challenging due to exponential search complexity and pervasive polysemanticity. The proposed Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD) framework reduces circuit discovery complexity from O(2^n) exhaustive enumeration to O(n^2 log n) through multi-resolution abstraction hierarchies and differentiable circuit search. The methodology integrates cross-layer transcoders for monosemantic feature extraction, graph neural network meta-learning for topology prediction, and causal intervention protocols for validation. Empirical evaluation spans GPT-2 variants, Llama-7B through Llama-70B, and Pythia suite models across algorithmic tasks and natural language benchmarks. On modular arithmetic tasks, the framework achieves up to 91% behavioral preservation ($\pm$2.3\% across runs) while maintaining interpretable subgraph sizes. Cross-architecture transfer experiments suggest that discovered circuits exhibit moderate structural similarity (averaging 67%) across model families, indicating potential shared computational patterns. These results provide preliminary foundations for interpretability at larger model scales while identifying significant limitations in current attribution methodologies that require future advances.

papers.title: Deeper Insights Without Updates: The Power of In-Context Learning Over Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning capture implicit patterns better than fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning outperforms fine-tuning in capturing implicit patterns in tasks, and the authors propose circuit shift theory to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning significantly outperforms fine-tuning in capturing implicit patterns within specific tasks and exhibits greater adaptability in problem-solving approaches, as evidenced by notable shifts in model circuits.
papers.key_findings:
ICL achieves higher accuracy than fine-tuning on implicit pattern detection tasks across models and tasks.
ICL is more robust to misleading data and out-of-distribution data compared to fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning plateaus quickly with more data, showing diminishing returns for implicit pattern detection.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods do not show significant improvement over full-parameter fine-tuning for implicit pattern detection.
ICL induces larger circuit shifts than fine-tuning, indicating a more significant change in the model's problem-solving approach.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability is constrained by the specific nature of the implicit pattern detection tasks, limited to certain domains.
Circuit Shift analysis relies on activation patching and sensitivity analysis, which require further refinement and validation across different models and tasks.
Computational resources required for fine-tuning, especially with large models, may limit the feasibility of such experiments in broader settings.
A detailed cost-benefit analysis comparing ICL and fine-tuning in terms of computational efficiency and performance is needed.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning and in-context learning (ICL) are two prevalent methods in imbuing large language models with task-specific knowledge. It is commonly believed that fine-tuning can surpass ICL given sufficient training samples as it allows the model to adjust its internal parameters based on the data. However, this paper presents a counterintuitive finding: For tasks with implicit patterns, ICL captures these patterns significantly better than fine-tuning. We developed several datasets featuring implicit patterns, such as sequences determining answers through parity or identifying reducible terms in calculations. We then evaluated the models' understanding of these patterns under both fine-tuning and ICL across models ranging from 0.5B to 7B parameters. The results indicate that models employing ICL can quickly grasp deep patterns and significantly improve accuracy. In contrast, fine-tuning, despite utilizing thousands of times more training samples than ICL, achieved only limited improvements. We also proposed circuit shift theory from a mechanistic interpretability's view to explain why ICL wins.

papers.title: Surgical Knowledge Rewrite in Compact LLMs: An 'Unlearn-then-Learn' Strategy with ($IA^3$) for Localized Factual Modulation and Catastrophic Forgetting Mitigation
papers.research_question: How to achieve precise knowledge editing in compact LLMs for conflicting factual updates while mitigating catastrophic forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mechanistically informed 'unlearn-then-learn' strategy with IA3 that achieves precise knowledge editing in compact LLMs, with high accuracy for new facts and minimal catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: The method enables deterministic, precise, and localized knowledge editing, advancing LLM knowledge management with enhanced safety and control.
papers.key_findings:
Achieves 98.50% accuracy for the new fact and 96.00% forget rate for the original fact.
Shows 72.00% F_control accuracy, significantly mitigating catastrophic forgetting compared to direct fine-tuning.
Demonstrates 'soft forgetting' where original knowledge is suppressed but remains latently accessible.
Outperforms direct fine-tuning methods like LoRA and IA3 in localization and fact modulation.
Uses circuit localization to inform targeted PEFT application for effective editing.
papers.limitation: The method may struggle to scale with sequential unlearning requests or larger forget sets in very large LLMs.
future_direction: Scalability of the strategy to larger LLMs
Further mechanistic insights into 'soft forgetting' and auditing unlearning
Potential for multi-fact and chained knowledge edits
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with dynamic knowledge updates, especially when new information conflicts with deeply embedded facts. Such conflicting factual edits often lead to two critical issues: resistance to adopting the new fact and severe catastrophic forgetting of unrelated knowledge. This paper introduces and evaluates a novel "unlearn-then-learn" strategy for precise knowledge editing in LLMs, leveraging the parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) technique, Infused Adapter by Inhibiting and Amplifying Inner Activations ($IA^3$). Crucially, this two-stage approach is powered by an initial circuit localization phase that identifies and targets the specific internal components responsible for encoding the conflicting fact. Through a rigorous experimental methodology on microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct, we demonstrate that this mechanistically informed two-stage approach achieves near-perfect accuracy (98.50%) for the new, modulated fact while simultaneously effectively suppressing the original conflicting fact (96.00% forget rate). Critically, our strategy exhibits unprecedented localization (72.00% F_control accuracy), dramatically mitigating catastrophic forgetting observed in direct fine-tuning approaches (which showed as low as ~20% F_control accuracy), a direct benefit of our targeted interpretability-guided intervention. Furthermore, qualitative analysis reveals a nuanced mechanism of "soft forgetting," where original knowledge is suppressed from default retrieval but remains latent and conditionally accessible, enhancing model safety and control. These findings represent a significant advancement towards precise, localized, and safe knowledge management in compact LLMs.

papers.title: The Rediscovery Hypothesis: Language Models Need to Meet Linguistics
papers.research_question: Is the rediscovery of linguistic knowledge mandatory for models that perform well on their pretraining tasks, or is it a side effect of overparameterization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces and supports the 'rediscovery hypothesis', which states that linguistic knowledge is a necessary condition for good language model performance, and provides an information-theoretic framework linking linguistic information to word prediction.
papers.conclusion: The rediscovery hypothesis is supported: linguistic knowledge is necessary for language models to perform well on their pretraining objectives, and the information-theoretic framework provides a way to quantify the importance of linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning language models up to 60-80% of weights does not significantly harm their performance on linguistic probing tasks, supporting the rediscovery hypothesis.
The drop in probing performance (e.g., for POS, NER, constituents) correlates with the increase in language modeling loss when models are pruned.
An information-theoretic framework shows that removing linguistic information from word representations degrades language modeling performance, and the degradation depends on the mutual information (ρ) between the linguistic property and the text.
Syntactic tasks (e.g., POS) are learned earlier and require less model capacity, while semantic tasks (e.g., NER, SRL) require more training and model size.
The proposed metric ρ reliably predicts the impact of a linguistic property on word prediction performance without needing the model or its representations.
papers.limitation:
Probing methodology cannot distinguish between information encoded in the pretrained vectors and information learned by the probing classifier.
Experiments and analysis are limited to the English language.
papers.abstract: There is an ongoing debate in the NLP community whether modern language models contain linguistic knowledge, recovered through so-called probes. In this paper, we study whether linguistic knowledge is a necessary condition for the good performance of modern language models, which we call the rediscovery hypothesis. In the first place, we show that language models that are significantly compressed but perform well on their pretraining objectives retain good scores when probed for linguistic structures. This result supports the rediscovery hypothesis and leads to the second contribution of our paper: an information-theoretic framework that relates language modeling objectives with linguistic information. This framework also provides a metric to measure the impact of linguistic information on the word prediction task. We reinforce our analytical results with various experiments, both on synthetic and on real NLP tasks in English.

papers.title: Core Knowledge Deficits in Multi-Modal Language Models
papers.research_question: Do multi-modal large language models lack core knowledge, i.e., rudimentary cognitive abilities that are innate in humans from early childhood?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the CoreCognition benchmark for evaluating core knowledge in MLLMs and finds that MLLMs exhibit significant deficits in low-level core abilities, show misaligned dependencies between abilities, and rely on shortcut learning rather than genuine understanding as they scale.
papers.conclusion: MLLMs exhibit significant deficits in core knowledge, and scaling does not lead to genuine understanding but instead increases reliance on shortcut learning.
papers.key_findings:
MLLMs consistently perform worse on low-level core abilities compared to high-level abilities.
MLLM performance on high-level abilities is not correlated with the underlying low-level abilities that support them.
MLLMs exhibit less, or even no, scalability on low-level abilities compared to high-level abilities as model parameters increase.
Models increasing in size exhibit core deficits and shortcut-taking behaviors rather than progressing toward conceptual understanding.
The proposed Concept Hacking method reveals MLLMs fail to achieve genuine core knowledge understanding and instead rely on shortcut learning.
papers.abstract: While Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate impressive abilities over high-level perception and reasoning, their robustness in the wild remains limited, often falling short on tasks that are intuitive and effortless for humans. We examine the hypothesis that these deficiencies stem from the absence of core knowledge--rudimentary cognitive abilities innate to humans from early childhood. To explore the core knowledge representation in MLLMs, we introduce CoreCognition, a large-scale benchmark encompassing 12 core knowledge concepts grounded in developmental cognitive science. We evaluate 230 models with 11 different prompts, leading to a total of 2,530 data points for analysis. Our experiments uncover four key findings, collectively demonstrating core knowledge deficits in MLLMs: they consistently underperform and show reduced, or even absent, scalability on low-level abilities relative to high-level ones. Finally, we propose Concept Hacking, a novel controlled evaluation method that reveals MLLMs fail to progress toward genuine core knowledge understanding, but instead rely on shortcut learning as they scale.

papers.title: Knowledge Swapping via Learning and Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can a pretrained model selectively forget user-specified information, retain essential knowledge, and acquire new knowledge simultaneously? What is the optimal order for the learning and forgetting processes?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Knowledge Swapping task and proposes a Learning Before Forgetting strategy, based on the insight that incremental learning progresses from low-level to high-level features while forgetting occurs in the opposite direction, which leads to more stable and effective knowledge regulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Knowledge Swapping task and the Learning Before Forgetting strategy provide an effective framework for selectively regulating model knowledge, enabling simultaneous forgetting, retention, and learning, which is validated across multiple vision tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Incremental learning typically progresses from low-level representations to higher-level semantic features, whereas targeted forgetting tends to occur in the opposite direction—starting from high-level semantics and moving down to low-level features.
The Learning Before Forgetting strategy (learning new tasks first, then performing selective forgetting) yields significantly better performance than the reverse order, as it confines forgetting to high-level semantics and avoids perturbing updated low-level distributions.
The proposed method, using LoRA-based fine-tuning with group sparse regularization, effectively achieves the three objectives of knowledge swapping: forgetting specified knowledge, retaining core knowledge, and learning new knowledge.
Experiments on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks validate the effectiveness of the Learning Before Forgetting strategy across different models and datasets.
The difficulty of learning new knowledge and forgetting old knowledge varies across different categories, suggesting an area for future exploration.
papers.limitation: The difficulty of learning new knowledge and forgetting old knowledge varies across different categories.
future_direction: Explore and analyze the difficulty of forgetting specific knowledge and learning new knowledge of categories.
papers.abstract: We introduce \textbf{Knowledge Swapping}, a novel task designed to selectively regulate knowledge of a pretrained model by enabling the forgetting of user\-specified information, retaining essential knowledge, and acquiring new knowledge simultaneously. By delving into the analysis of knock-on feature hierarchy, we find that incremental learning typically progresses from low\-level representations to higher\-level semantics, whereas forgetting tends to occur in the opposite direction\-starting from high-level semantics and moving down to low-level features. Building upon this, we propose to benchmark the knowledge swapping task with the strategy of \textit{Learning Before Forgetting}. Comprehensive experiments on various tasks like image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation validate the effectiveness of the proposed strategy.
